extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism students, and professional journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and describe the enduring cultural, political, and institutional values that journalists and news organizations use (implicitly) to decide what is newsworthy. The page catalogs these values and gives examples of how they shape coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Altruistic Democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The news implies that politics should follow a course based on the public interest and public service; politics is treated as a contest identifying winners and losers but both are expected to be scrupulously honest, efficient, and dedicated to the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and signals: stories about financial corruption, nepotism, patronage, logrolling, and 'deals' are routinely newsworthy; deviations from officials' stated honesty (e.g., campaign promises) become headlines (Eugene McCarthy, George McGovern, Jimmy Carter). Citizens are expected to participate altruistically ("grassroots activity" is complimentary), while organized lobbying and pressure groups are treated with suspicion. The news endorses formal constitutional norms and defends democratic theory against informal practices. Selective attention: press freedom and related civil liberties receive high attention, while some other protections (e.g., due process for criminals) are less newsworthy. Examples/anti-patterns: Secretary Califano's chef (spartan tastes expected of officials) is news; routine economic barriers to democratic access are underreported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endorsement of Official Norms (formal norms derived from the Constitution)
rubrics_metrics.description: The news sets up formal norms and structures of democratic institutions as standards (those established by the Founding Fathers) and treats violations of these official norms as newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The news tends to defend these formal norms and is suspicious of informal power-allocation structures. It selectively tracks violations (e.g., freedom of the press and civil liberties have been frequent national stories; other protections may be undercovered). Coverage often frames news as violations against these official norms without always making the underlying values explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption of Separation Between Polity and Economy
rubrics_metrics.description: News often assumes the polity and the economy are separate and independent; economic power and poverty are treated as less central to the democratic ideal than political conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: reporting notices candidates' wealth or campaign funding but gives less attention to the relationship between poverty and political power or access. Government intervention in the economy is more newsworthy than private industry's influence on government (public subsidy of private firms is often unremarked). This leads to inattention to economic obstacles to realizing democratic ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsible Capitalism
rubrics_metrics.description: The news posture toward the economy presumes businessmen will compete to create prosperity for all but should refrain from unreasonable profits and gross exploitation; small/family firms and entrepreneurship are idealized, and bigness (monopoly, oligopoly) is viewed suspiciously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage patterns: economic growth is positive unless it causes inflation, pollution, historic destruction, or job loss; business failures are tolerated more than government experiment failures; regulators and welfare programs are scrutinized (welfare cheaters highlighted). Foreign socialist economies are criticized for threats to private property and liberties; socialist critiques at home are underreported. Examples: Time's longer treatment of government regulation vs shorter business-item coverage (GM engine refunds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Small-town Pastoralism
rubrics_metrics.description: News favors small towns and rural/market-town values—cohesiveness, friendliness, slow pace, and an imagined past—over large cities or impersonal bigness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manifestations: nostalgic features about small towns and mourning the loss of traditional places/technologies; suburbs often receive negative coverage or are underreported despite population size; developers and 'urban' problems are criticized. Stories judge city neighborhoods by their ability to retain 'small-town' qualities. The virtue of smallness also expresses a preference for nature and resistance to large-scale development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valorization of Tradition and Old Technology
rubrics_metrics.description: The news celebrates tradition and older technologies as symbols of a simpler, more controllable life, and treats their loss sentimentally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: features on the closing of craftsmanship businesses, berthing of ocean liners, elimination of old railroads; old technology is romanticized while new technology is portrayed as potentially dehumanizing. This links to broader pastoral and smallness values and is often nostalgic rather than critical-analytic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individualism
rubrics_metrics.description: A central news value is preserving individual freedom against encroachment by nation or society; coverage focuses on people rather than groups and admires self-made, heroic individuals who overcome adversity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators: interest in explorers, astronauts, scientists, and individuals overcoming poverty or bureaucracy; news emphasizes personal stories over group identities. Threats to individualism (computers, data banks, socialism) are framed as dangers. The news values the 'work ethic' and is concerned about conformity or loss of individual initiative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderatism
rubrics_metrics.description: The news ideology favors moderation and discredits excess or extremism; extremes are discouraged whether they represent excess or complete abstention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices: groups or individuals perceived as extremists (atheists, religious fanatics, radical movements) are treated pejoratively; both conspicuous consumers and anti-consumer 'hippies' are criticized. In politics, ideologues are suspect while completely unprincipled actors are also distrusted. Moderate solutions and balanced actors are valorized; the effective loner can be a hero but unsuccessful mavericks are pejoratively labeled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social Order and National Leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: News tends to divide stories into 'disorder news' (threats to order and efforts to restore it) and routine coverage of leading public officials; this reflects values placed on social order and presidential/national leadership in preserving it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: the news emphasizes both detection of threats and the visible restoration of order by officials. The stability of leadership (e.g., quick orderly transitions after crises) is repeatedly used as an index of national order and reassurance to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of Disorder News (natural, technological, social, moral)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disorder stories are usefully classified into four categories: natural (natural disasters and accidents attributed to nature), technological (accidents not ascribable to nature), social (disturbances of public peace, violence, and institutional deterioration), and moral (transgressions of laws and mores).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories are fluid in practice: events can shift categories as new information emerges (e.g., arson reclassifies a fire). Each category carries different news values and ways of reporting (e.g., emphasis on victims, causes, or restoration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Social Disorder News (treatment of demonstrations and unrest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Domestic social disorder stories (e.g., ghetto disturbances, anti-war marches) are often framed as threats to social order; large demonstrations are treated as potentially dangerous, with 'trouble' defined as violent confrontation, especially against police or property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage tendencies: early focus on unusual-looking participants, visual cues of threat; emphasis on violence or potential for violence; a shift over time (e.g., post-1968) toward viewing demonstrators as protesters and paying attention to nonviolent, mainstream participants. News also often focuses heavily on order-restoration (police/army actions) rather than on causes of disorder; empirical example: Kerner Commission finding that much coverage emphasized order restoration over riot actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Disorder News (exposes and investigative reporting)
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral disorder story tradition centers on exposes that reveal legal or moral transgressions, especially by public officials and prestigious individuals not expected to misbehave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features: investigative exposes (e.g., Watergate, CIA/FBI scandals) are structured to identify transgressors and force defensive responses; routine crimes and political practices (logrolling, patronage, campaign promise violations) are also framed as moral disorder. Media function as guardians of moral order—camera presence can suppress wrongdoing or cause performative behavior; refusal to be interviewed is reported and can imply guilt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective Visibility and Performance Effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The news does not neutrally record events; its presence and framing change behavior and which practices become visible as moral disorder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: when reporters or cameras arrive institutions 'spruce up' or hide abuses; some abuses (e.g., routine police brutality) were historically underreported until visibility increased. The news both uncovers and shapes moral narratives, sometimes aggregating disparate acts into a single scandal.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Nature and Subjectivity of 'Order' (whose order?)
rubrics_metrics.description: Order is not unitary: different social groups define 'order' differently (e.g., affluent people view slums as orderly if disturbances don't spill into their districts; slum dwellers experience order as non-exploitative conditions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for coverage: what the news treats as disorder or order depends on whose perspective is privileged; the news' conception of order varies across contexts (natural disaster, technological accident, social unrest) and shapes what aspects are emphasized (preservation of life/property vs ecological or systemic concerns). Example: in natural disaster coverage order = preservation of life and property; in social contexts, order may center on family stability or adolescent autonomy depending on viewpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual Newsworthiness: Type-Specific Priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: The news defines newsworthiness within disorder types differently; certain incidents (e.g., plane crashes) are more newsworthy than other equally deadly but less sensational events (e.g., tenement furnace deaths).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reflects whose order is being seen as violated and the cultural salience of particular events; selection is influenced by spectacularity, affected populations, and perceived threat to broader social order.
